textbookText: Figure: 1.1.1 Classification of carbohydrate 1. Monosaccharides (CnH2nOn) Monosaccharides are the simplest forms of carbohydrates and cannot be broken down into smaller units. Some common examples are glucose, fructose, and galactose. Structurally, monosaccharides are composed of polyhydroxy compounds, with all carbon atoms having a hydroxyl group, except one, which contains either an aldehyde or a ketone group. Monosaccharides with free aldehyde and ketone groups are termed reducing sugars because they can reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ form. They are highly soluble in water and taste sweet. Do you know? Derived monosaccharides are the modified monosaccharides obtained by alteration (the addition or removal) of functional groups. Key derivatives include deoxy sugar (e.g., deoxyribose of DNA), amino sugars (e.g., glucosamine), sugar acid (e.g., ascorbic acid), and sugar alcohol (e.g., mannitol). E.g.
